newsitem.title: USA: NYC shrugs off court ruling rejecting water sale.
newsitem.headline: NYC shrugs off court ruling rejecting water sale.

text.p: The Giuliani Administration of New York City shrugged off a court's decision killing its plans to sell the city's water and sewer system, saying that it had sufficient borrowing authority to fill any gaps.

New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani had been counting on using about $1 billion of the funds that would have been raised by selling the water system to finance a range of capital projects, with the largest amount, $600 million, included in the fiscal 11997 budget, which ends on June 30.
But Deputy Mayor Randy Mastro, told Reuters in a telephone interview: "This has no impact on our operating budget because we had already budgeted for an adverse court decision."
He added New York City's capital plan also was unaffected because the city found enough room under its state-imposed debt ceiling to carry it through the rest of the fiscal 1997 year.

And looking ahead, New York City will be able to borrow an extra $7.5 billion over the next four years by using the new, New York City Transitional Financing Authority, whose creation Albany recently agreed to, as a way to let the city skirt its debt cap. This extra capacity also helps relieve the pressure on the city's capital plan.

The Giuliani Administration had planned to divide the remaining $400 million of the $1 billion part of the water sale proceeds between fiscal 1998 and fiscal 1999, with about $200 million budgeted for each fiscal year, Mastro said.

New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi had blocked the city from selling the water system, which it has owned for 150 years, by saying he would decline to approve the $2.3 billion bond sale that was part of the transaction. Each day, the city's water system pumps about 1.5 billion gallons of water to eight million people who live in New York City and Westchester County.

Mayor Rudolph Giuliani took the fight over the water system to court, but the state's highest court on Thursday rejected the plan, saying the Water Finance Authority could only sell bonds for water projects and corporate purposes.

The Deputy Mayor added that the Giuliani Administration would study the various proposals being put forward to fill any shortfall. For example, Alan Hevesi, the city comptroller, has said the city should use other planned asset sales, like disposing of the Coliseum in midtown, to provide pay-as-you-go financing.

And the City Council said it again would recommend privatizing waste treatment plants, a proposal that it said first triggered the mayor's interest in selling the water system when it raised the issue in March, 1994. Mastro, while noting that the Giuliani Administration worked closely with the City Council, said that its initial review of this plan had suggested that the policy would not save the city money.
